facts.text: A base rate describes how often an event happens in normal operation; an exposure-based rate expresses that frequency per unit of exposure, such as false alarms per 1,000 operating hours, rather than per staged test.
facts.quote: A base rate is how often something happens in normal operation, and an exposure-based rate expresses it per unit of exposure, such as false alarms per 1,000 operating hours, rather than per staged test.

facts.text: Detection is measured per encounter, whereas false alarms and unnecessary braking require different denominators because they can occur with no object or danger. The booklet measures false alarms and unnecessary braking per operating hour, per work cycle or per object-free encounter.
facts.quote: The booklet therefore measures them per operating hour, per work cycle or per object-free encounter

facts.text: Exposure hours used to measure false alarms and unnecessary braking must represent normal operation; the booklet usually obtains these hours through shadow mode on customer sites.
facts.quote: insists that the hours be representative operation, usually gathered by shadow mode on customer sites.

facts.text: Ruff's study for NIOSH (the United States National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health) recorded 580 alarms from a haul-truck radar system over seven days and 618 reversals: 102 false alarms, 243 nuisance alarms about known objects, and only 235 alarms (41 percent) warranting action.
facts.quote: 580 alarms sounded over seven days and 618 reversals; 102 were false, 243 were nuisance alarms about known objects, and only 235 (41 percent) warranted action.

facts.text: Staged tests with targets would not have revealed the proportion of alarms warranting action in Ruff's NIOSH haul-truck radar study.
facts.quote: Staged tests with targets would never have revealed that ratio

facts.text: If false alarms follow a steady random rate—a homogeneous Poisson process—and zero events are observed in T hours, the approximate 95 percent upper bound on the event rate is 3 divided by T.
facts.quote: If false alarms occur at a steady random rate (a homogeneous Poisson process) and none is seen in T hours, the 95 percent upper bound on the rate is about 3 divided by T.

facts.text: Under the steady random-rate assumption, 300 hours with no unnecessary brake supports a rate below 1 per 100 hours, and 3,000 event-free hours supports a rate below 1 per 1,000 hours, using the approximate 95 percent upper bound.
facts.quote: So 300 hours with no unnecessary brake supports "fewer than 1 per 100 hours", and 3,000 hours supports "fewer than 1 per 1,000 hours".

facts.text: Under the steady random-rate assumption, observing two events in T hours raises the approximate 95 percent upper bound on the event rate to 6.3 divided by T.
facts.quote: With two events in T hours the bound rises to about 6.3 divided by T.

facts.text: Chapter 7 states that demonstrating fewer than 0.1 false alarms per hour requires at least 30 failure-free hours for each condition claimed.
facts.quote: Chapter 7 gives the same arithmetic: fewer than 0.1 false alarms per hour needs at least 30 failure-free hours, per condition claimed

facts.text: False alarms at mines and construction sites can cluster into bursts triggered by bucket passes or dust clouds; clustering violates the steady-rate assumption used for the 3-divided-by-T rate bound.
facts.quote: False alarms cluster: every bucket pass or dust cloud may trigger a burst. Clustering breaks the steady-rate assumption

facts.text: Before relying on the 3-divided-by-T rate bound, the booklet recommends checking the steady-rate assumption and, where it fails, using work-cycle or site blocks, overdispersed count models or block bootstrap methods.
facts.quote: the booklet advises checking it and, where it fails, using work-cycle or site blocks, overdispersed count models or block bootstrap methods before relying on 3 divided by T

facts.text: Chapter 3 found no off-road standard or regulation specifying fleet-statistical measures such as false alarms per operating hour and unnecessary brake events per hour; the collision mitigation program must define and defend its own measures.
facts.quote: Chapter 3 found that fleet-statistical measures such as false alarms per operating hour and unnecessary brake events per hour appear in no off-road standard or regulation, so the program must define and defend its own.

facts.text: Nuisance braking is a safety problem because operators disable systems that stop them too often; the exposure-based nuisance-braking rate is therefore a safety target, not merely a comfort target.
facts.quote: Nuisance braking is also a safety problem, because operators disable systems that stop them too often, which makes the exposure-based rate a safety target and not only a comfort one
